--- title: "Lecture 7" execute: freeze: auto # re-render only when source changes format: revealjs: theme: serif incremental: true preview-links: auto chalkboard: true margin: 0 width: 1080 engine: julia julia: exeflags: ["--project=../PopGen25"] bibliography: references.bib --- ## Quantitative trait evolution {.smaller} Now that we have a better feeling for how all of the different processes impact the evolution in alleles, it's worth thinking about quantitative traits in general. . . . Today we'll talk about how genetic variation for traits is distributed, and what this tells us about their evolution. . . . We'll talk about how we can identify causal alleles for traits, and why sometimes that is either impossible, or extra complicated. . . . We'll end by considering the *ultimate* trait - fitness, and how fitness changes as populations evovle (and what that can teach us about evolution of reproductive isolation, hybridization, etc.) ## Last time Last week we talked about the Breeder's equation. $$ R = S h^2 = S \frac{V_A}{V_P} $$ . . . This equation describes how a trait changes based on changes in the average among those who mated vs the whole population, and how much of that change is heritable. . . . We did not discuss how $V_A$ changes in response to selection. ## Change in genetic variability due to selection {.smaller} Let's think through multiple cases: . . . Take directional selection, with all alleles being nice additive values for trait: decreases . . . Take directional selection, but all alleles are overdominant: decreases even faster. . . . Stabilizing selection, additive values: decreases as different alleles become fixed. . . . Stabilizing and overdominance: while no alleles are fixed, $V_A$ goes to 0. ## Remember that we care about the *additive* genetic variation ::: {#2 .cell execution_count=1} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ## Renewing $V_A$ Mutations re-introduce genetic variation for a trait. . . . Because they are *extremely* rare when they enter the population, most change in allele frequencies leads to additive effects. . . . So, most new mutations increase additive genetic variation for a trait. . . . Long-term - $V_A$ will settle on a value depending on both new mutations and strength of selection. ## Some counter-factuals {.smaller} Just because genetic variation decreases due to selection, does not mean it disappears. ::: {#4 .cell execution_count=1} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ## But it *can* have limits ::: {#6 .cell execution_count=1} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ## But it *is* reversible ::: {#8 .cell execution_count=1} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ## Long term change re-measured It's worth considering that changing by 1% oil content may be much easier when oil content is high than when it is low. . . . We instead consider the $log(\frac{X_1}{X_2})$, where $X_1$ is the starting trait value, and $X_2$ is the ending one. . . . What's often noticed on this scale is that change is *not* linear: change might be faster initially, and slow down later. . . . Not the case in corn data! ## In oil data ::: {#10 .cell execution_count=1} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ## LTEE of fitness It *is* the case for change in fitness in Lenski's long term *E. coli* evolution. ![](https://www.science.org/cms/10.1126/science.1243357/asset/6f1f047b-9303-4c88-bc7c-ebd32d50508d/assets/graphic/342_1364_f2.jpeg){width="1200"} . . . Why? ## Fisher's Geometric Model ::: {#12 .cell execution_count=1} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ## When closer to optimum ::: {#14 .cell execution_count=1} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ## When *really* close to optimum ::: {#16 .cell execution_count=1} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ## So, expectation when adapting to new optimum When populations adapt to a new optimum, the first fixed mutations are expected to have large effects. . . . Mutations fixed later in the process have increasingly smaller effects, as large effect mutations become increasingly likely to be deleterious. . . . Vanishingly unlikely that population ever fully adapts to optimum, and will instead reach a point where selection is about as strong as drift. ## How do we detect phenotypic selection? {.smaller} Knowing if some traits are under directional or stabilizing selection might be important. . . . Could just compare many related species and see if your species of interest is "extreme" for a trait value. . . . The problem is that traits do no evolve independently - correlated change due to shared ancestry. . . . So, even if evolution is not directed, there may be differences along the phylogeny that look significant. . . . The whole field of phylogenetic comparative methods is there to help you. ## Phylogenetic comparative methods {.smaller} Easiest to show the problem using multiple trait correlations. . . . ::: {#18 .cell execution_count=1} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ## PIC example {.smaller} In this case - no actual correlation between traits (or directionality): both simulated under Brownian-Motion. . . . One simple way to account for shared history: Phylogenetically independent contrasts. . . . Calculate differences between each branch, and compare these. ::: {#20 .cell execution_count=1} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ## Brownian motion as a null model We can also use the expectations from Brownian motion to see if traits are evolving faster/slower than expected. . . . Ideally, we can identify rates across the tree, and find _rate shifts_: branches on which evolutionary rates have changed. . . . Without the evolutionary context - an extreme trait value could just be a result of drift . . . Especially true if trait is highly polygenic - lots of small random changes can lead to big overall differences. ## How can we identify genetic structure of traits? Understanding the genetic basis of adaptive traits is not as straightforward as it may seem. . . . We covered this in part already - you can look at regions with differences between closely related species for selection, but not guaranteed to link to your trait. . . . If you can interbreed - QTL. . . . If still polymorphic - GWAS. ## Genome Wide Association Studies Genome wide association studies essentially take genotypes of many individuals in a population along with their phenotypes, and return the correlation between each genotype and the phenotype of interest. . . . At its heart - simple linear regression! . . . More broadly - can take advantage of known inheritance patterns (pedigrees) to account for population structure. ## GWAS example ::: {#22 .cell execution_count=1} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ## Accounting for population structure The problem with just running a linear model is that some correlations exist for other reasons. . . . LD with the actual causal locus. . . . Correlation with environmental explanatory variable. ## Back to example ::: {#24 .cell execution_count=1} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ## More details Most GWAS approaches are structured as linear mixed models: $$ z = x + C + \epsilon $$ Where $x$ is the genotype at a site, $C$ is a covariate matrix, and $\epsilon$ is noise. . . . For many analyses, the covariate will be the first few PCs of a PCA of the data. Why? . . . Ideally, these would be ancestry correlations, but as you've seen, these can be hard to estimate. ## Some things you can't account for {.smaller} Even when GWAS is performed _perfectly_, we can still have a lot of missing information. . . . "Missing heritability" in height. Height about 80% heritable in worst case. . . . Tons of studies, 5.4 million sequences, and we have 12k variants explaining about 55% of variation. . . . Multiple issues: low power to detect effects of rare variants, correction for structure exclude GxE effects, etc. . . . Height is also a complex trait affected by many other selected traits (nutrition,immunity). . . . Predictions harder when there is multi-trait selection and alleles are pleiotropic. ## Multi-trait correlations and selection We've covered the Breeder's Equation, but an equally important result is Lande's Multivariate Breeder's Equation: $$ \Delta \bar{Z} = GP^{-1}S = G \beta $$ . . . Here, $G$ is the genetic variance-covariance matrix, $P$ is the phenotypic covariance matrix and $S$ is the selection gradient. $\beta$ is the vector of directional selection gradients. $\beta$ is a fraction of the phenotypic variance that is selected. ## A quick example $$ \Delta \bar{Z} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0.6 \\ 0.6 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -0.1 \end{bmatrix} \approxeq \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1/2 \end{bmatrix} $$ ## What does that mean Traits change in proportion to genetic co-variation. . . . A trait can move in the opposite direction of its optimum, if selection on a different trait is stronger and correlations are strong. . . . Most famously: Darwin's Finches ## Darwin's Finches {.smaller} Galapagos struck by a drought in 1976. Peter and Rosemary Grant measured \~700 finches before the drought, and kept track of survivors. | Trait | Before drought average | After drought average | |-------------|------------------------|-----------------------| | Weight | 16.06 | 17.13 | | Bill length | 10.63 | 10.95 | | Bill depth | 9.21 | 9.70 | . . . From the first glance - looks like positive selection on all three traits. . . . If we account for genetic covariance in traits, we can calculate $\beta$. ## Inferred selection | Trait | $\beta$ | |-------------|---------| | Weight | 0.477 | | Bill length | -0.144 | | Bill depth | 0.528 | . . . Because bill length and depth are highly correlated, stronger selection wins out. ## Across species variation ![Beausoleil et al. 2023](https://oup.silverchair-cdn.com/oup/backfile/Content_public/Journal/evolut/77/12/10.1093_evolut_qpad160/3/m_qpad160_fig1.jpeg?Expires=1763470337&Signature=dgXV2aEUJ6XkJaQK-ORDPSLgFwwZJxsps4O1AMkQH0OifbCI9c9EJB8BBmLKVsCAo0gPcEFYHxEU1sZN48xYmxB0-K~HvhnbB-HubYP-a921j6tSrm-Itulk35yG-47CF7YwcgbLdcsk9YFaB-4gx1Oz~uZLo6TP589t5mF-2RqvQaKL3DfzAl7eUlbtOicaeS~TQ7MRMuzn1JCA~A5L2B6p-s9cHm8VIeBN1qQFNY~oQjwXABzr44R~cEh9nihRqAGGQM21mLedCvyUEbrAE0beI3bG7tM10B8qLg5x1AR54XcZrZpvd6KaZX82neT17cE8gcSUdJ5J0QkHCasg9w__&Key-Pair-Id=APKAIE5G5CRDK6RD3PGA) ## Some fun thoughts When we think about evolvability, we need to consider the mean of the population. . . . Even when multiple alternate strategies have are different fitness peaks with deep valleys between - the population may be able to contain both peaks. . . . Reproductive isolation due to alternate strategies requires the peaks to be far apart, or the valleys very deep. ## More consequences {.smaller} Whether populations can evolve to different parts of a fitness landscape depends on *how* the traits are correlated. . . . ![example](https://bio.libretexts.org/@api/deki/files/64592/clipboard_ed8dd74271e352ff1ddfeff98687f6ec8.png?revision=1&size=bestfit&width=637&height=350) ## Visually: Simulation courtesy of Diogo Melo: [link](https://curso-genevol.shinyapps.io/superficie-adaptativa/) ## Consequences for interpreting data. If a trait you are studying is controlled by many alleles, and is potentially linked to other traits under selection, inference of evolutionary patterns becomes increasingly difficult. . . . If the trait is highly polygenic, each individual allele might have low signal. . . . If the alleles controlling the trait are highly pleiotropic - signal may be dampened depending on how trait is measured. . . . If multiple traits genetically covariated and one under very strong selection - the other will have low polymorphism, so low power to detect causal alleles. ## The ultimate complex trait - fitness We've already mentioned this, but fitness is a highly composite trait. . . . Likely affected to some degree by more or less every allele *and* tied to most traits. . . . Yet, we can often detect clear signals of adaptation, with alleles showing strong relationships w/fitness. . . . So, even when you study complex traits, you *can* identify the causal alleles. But optimal values may be harder to find. ## How common is this worry of complex genetic underpinnings of traits? {.smaller} There are certainly some traits with simple genetic control (e.g. 1-2 alleles of strong effect). . . . The slowly building consensus is that many traits of interest may in fact be "omnigenic" - affected to some degree by pretty much any allele in the genome. . . . Most alleles either influence trait, or linked to something that does. . . . In practice, each location is at least somewhat correlated to any continuous trait of interest. . . . Data primarily coming from _D. melanogaster_, _S. cerevisiae_ : large population sizes, rapid generation times, easy for a cell division rate to influence most traits. . . . Might not be the case for other organisms, especially with smaller pop sizes and longer generation times. ## Back to Speciation Let's consider for a moment two populations evolving to the _same_ peak. . . . Even though they will both evolve similar trait values, _how_ they control these traits may be different. . . . Simplest case: two traits, single optimum. . . . See chalkboard ## Speciation in Fisher's Geometric Model {.smaller} Fisher's Geometric Model can generate some nice predictions about how fitness between different groups will change as they diverge, _even if they evolve to the same peak_. . . . Notably - fitness in hybrids will decrease because of different combinations of alleles shifting you off of the optimum. . . . Cool aspects: - Makes relatively simple assumptions about the fitness landscape - Generates some known patterns of speciation biology - Can be parameterized using known hybrid fitness data - Can explain hybrid speciation Weaknesses: - Many more assumptions needed to get other classic results - Allows for heterosis, but only if parents are both unfit - Strong assumptions about the effect size of mutations, especially for some of the big results ## Alternatives to explain speciation Bateson-Dobzhansky-Muller Incompatibilities! . . . More on this next week, as we chat about all of the processes interplaying with each other for changes in allele frequencies. . . . The week after, we'll talk more about how the interplay of all of the processes results in trait evolution. . . . Finally, we'll chat about the geneology of all alleles including all of these processes - the Ancestral Recombination Graph. We'll discuss some approaches to estimating it, and what to do once you have it. ## Student's Choice The last two weeks we've reserved for student's choice of topics. . . . I'll send out a survey with several topics I would normally include but haven't had the time for, but I'll leave a blank for whatever your heart desires. . . . We'll lock in favorite options next week. . . . Strong caveat - if it's something I've never worked on, might not be as good of a lecture/lab. ## Paper for this week {.smaller} Chen and Pannell - completely optional, but cool study. . . . Examine how the fitness of different plants changes as they produce varying amounts of male/female flowers. . . . The optimum is _not_ to specialize in one or the other - indeed, the dynamics are quite complex. . . . Male flower production correlated with hermaphroditic flower production, so optimum becomes complex. . . . Further - self-fertilization can lead to inbreeding, so different optima depending on whether inbreeding is considered or ignored.
